blocks.title: Definitions of Trigonometric Functions of Any Angle
teacherCues: Draw an angle in standard position with terminal side passing through a point (x, y). Ask: How do we find r? How does this generalize the acute definitions?
Write the six trig function definitions in terms of x, y, r. Have students identify which functions are undefined when x = 0 or y = 0.

discoveryHook.scenario: A plane takes off and climbs at an angle. The control tower tracks its position using coordinates (x, y) relative to the tower. Even if the angle is more than 90°, the sine and cosine of that angle still describe the plane's position relative to the hypotenuse distance r. Trigonometry extends naturally to any angle!

explanation: Let $ \theta $ be an angle in standard position with a point $ (x, y) $ on its terminal side. Define $ r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} $ (always positive).
The six trig functions for any angle are: $$ \sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} \ (x \neq 0) $$

$$ \csc	heta =  rac{r}{y} \ (y 
eq 0), \quad \sec	heta =  rac{r}{x} \ (x 
eq 0), \quad \cot	heta =  rac{x}{y} \ (y 
eq 0) $$
$ \tan\theta $ and $ \sec\theta $ are undefined when $ x = 0 $ (terminal side on y‑axis). $ \cot\theta $ and $ \csc\theta $ are undefined when $ y = 0 $ (terminal side on x‑axis).
These definitions coincide with the acute triangle definitions when $ \theta $ is acute.

visuals.title: General Trig Function Definitions
visuals.caption: r = sqrt(x² + y²) is always positive.

formulaCard.title: Coordinates to Trig Functions
notes: r is the distance from origin to (x, y).
Signs of x, y determine sign of functions.

examples.title: Example A — Given a Point on Terminal Side
examples.prompt: Let (-3, 4) be on the terminal side of θ. Find sin θ, cos θ, tan θ.

examples.title: Example B — Undefined Functions
examples.prompt: For θ = 90°, what point could you use on the terminal side? Which functions are undefined?
examples.peerPrompt: Without looking back, tell a partner: Why are tan 90° and sec 90° undefined?
steps: Choose point (0, 1) on terminal side, r = 1.
tan θ = y/x = 1/0 (undefined); sec θ = r/x = 1/0 (undefined).
sin θ = 1, cos θ = 0 are defined.

examples.title: Example C — Find Function Values
examples.prompt: Let (-2, -3) be on the terminal side of θ. Find cos θ and csc θ.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget r
confusionCorner.body: Always compute r first. r is always positive; x and y can be negative. The signs of the trig functions come from the signs of x and y, not from r.

questions.prompt: In the definition $ \sin\theta = \frac{y}{r} $, r is the distance from the ___ to the point (x, y).
questions.feedbackIfWrong: r is the distance from the origin.

questions.prompt: If (3, -4) is on terminal side of θ, what is sin θ? (Fraction like '4/5' or '-4/5'.)
For θ = 180°, what is tan θ? (Number or 'undefined'.)

blocks.title: Signs of Trigonometric Functions by Quadrant
teacherCues: Draw coordinate axes and label quadrants. Ask: In which quadrants is x positive? y positive?
Write 'All Students Take Calculus' on the board and ask students to identify which functions are positive in each quadrant.

discoveryHook.scenario: A submarine's sonar detects an object at coordinates (negative, negative) — deep and to the left. The sine and cosine of the angle to that object are both negative. Knowing the sign pattern helps the navigator instantly determine the quadrant without calculating the angle.

explanation: Because r > 0, the sign of each trig function depends solely on the signs of x and y.
$ \sin\theta = y/r $: positive when y > 0 (Quadrants I, II); negative when y < 0 (III, IV).
$ \cos\theta = x/r $: positive when x > 0 (I, IV); negative when x < 0 (II, III).
$ \tan\theta = y/x $: positive when x and y have same sign (I, III); negative when signs differ (II, IV).
Mnemonic: 'All Students Take Calculus' – A (All positive in I), S (Sine in II), T (Tangent in III), C (Cosine in IV).

visuals.title: Quadrant Signs for Trig Functions
visuals.caption: Reciprocals have same signs as originals.

examples.title: Example A — Determine Quadrant from Signs
examples.prompt: If sin θ > 0 and cos θ < 0, in which quadrant does θ lie?
steps: sin positive → y > 0 (Quadrants I or II).
cos negative → x < 0 (Quadrants II or III).

examples.title: Example B — Sign of tan θ Given Quadrant
examples.prompt: θ is in Quadrant III. What is the sign of tan θ?
examples.peerPrompt: Recite 'All Students Take Calculus' to a partner and explain which function is positive in III.
steps: In Quadrant III, both x and y are negative.
So tan θ > 0 in Quadrant III.

examples.title: Example C — Finding Function Sign
examples.prompt: If cos θ = 0.6 and tan θ < 0, find the sign of sin θ.
steps: cos θ positive → θ in I or IV.
tan θ negative → θ in II or IV.
So θ is in Quadrant IV, where y < 0 → sin θ negative.

confusionCorner.title: Reciprocal Same Sign
confusionCorner.body: The reciprocal functions csc, sec, cot always have the same sign as sin, cos, tan because they are just 1 over the function. Don't overthink them — just look at the original function.

questions.prompt: In which quadrant are both sin θ and cos θ negative? (Answer I, II, III, or IV.)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Both are negative only in Quadrant III.

questions.prompt: According to the mnemonic, in Quadrant IV, only ___ and its reciprocal are positive.
hints: It's the function that is positive in Quadrant IV.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: In Quadrant IV, cosine and secant are positive.

questions.prompt: If tan θ < 0 and sin θ > 0, in which quadrant is θ? (I, II, III, IV?)
hints: tan negative: signs of x and y differ (II or IV).
questions.feedbackIfWrong: θ must be in Quadrant II.

blocks.title: Reference Angles
teacherCues: Draw an obtuse angle and its acute reference angle (the angle formed with the x-axis). Ask: How do we find this acute angle?
On the board, show formulas for each quadrant: Qi = θ, Qii = 180°-θ, Qiii = θ-180°, Qiv = 360°-θ.

discoveryHook.scenario: The sine of 150° is exactly the same as the sine of 30°, except for the sign. The acute reference angle lets us use the special triangle values we've already memorized for any angle in any quadrant.

explanation: A [[kw:reference angle]] $ \theta' $ is the acute angle formed by the terminal side of $ \theta $ and the horizontal axis (x‑axis).
Quadrant I: $ \theta' = \theta $.
Quadrant II: $ \theta' = 180° - \theta $ (or $ \pi - \theta $).
Quadrant III: $ \theta' = \theta - 180° $ (or $ \theta - \pi $).
Quadrant IV: $ \theta' = 360° - \theta $ (or $ 2\pi - \theta $).
The absolute values of trig functions at $ \theta $ equal the values at the reference angle $ \theta' $; the sign depends on the quadrant of $ \theta $.

visuals.title: Finding Reference Angles
visuals.caption: If θ is outside 0–360°, first find a coterminal angle within that range.

formulaCard.title: Reference Angle Formulas
formulaCard.formula: $$ \theta' = \begin{cases} \theta & \text{if } \theta \text{ in QI} \\ 180° - \theta & \text{if } \theta \text{ in QII} \\ \theta - 180° & \text{if } \theta \text{ in QIII} \\ 360° - \theta & \text{if } \theta \text{ in QIV} \end{cases} $$
notes: Use radian equivalents: π instead of 180°, 2π instead of 360°.

examples.title: Example A — Reference Angle for 210°
examples.prompt: Find the reference angle for θ = 210°.

examples.title: Example B — Reference Angle in Radians
examples.prompt: Find the reference angle for θ = 5π/3.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Which quadrant is 5π/3 in? What formula do you use?

examples.title: Example C — Negative Angle
examples.prompt: Find the reference angle for θ = -135°.

confusionCorner.title: Always Acute
confusionCorner.body: A reference angle is always between 0° and 90° (0 and π/2). If your result is larger than 90°, you used the wrong formula. Check your quadrant!

questions.prompt: What is the reference angle for 120°? (Just the number.)
For an angle in Quadrant IV, the reference angle is found by ___ minus θ.
hints: Subtract the given angle from the full revolution.

questions.prompt: Find the reference angle for θ = 7π/4. (Answer in terms of pi, like 'pi/4'.)

blocks.title: Evaluating Trigonometric Functions Using Reference Angles
teacherCues: Show sin 150°: reference angle = 30°, sin 30° = 1/2, quadrant II sin positive → sin 150° = 1/2.
Ask students to evaluate cos 210° using reference angle and quadrant sign.

discoveryHook.scenario: Your GPS calculates your heading as 225°. The cosine of this angle is negative because your x-coordinate is negative (westward). By using the reference angle of 45°, the GPS quickly computes cos 225° = -√2/2 without needing a calculator.

explanation: To evaluate a trig function at any angle θ:
1. Find the reference angle θ' (acute).
2. Determine the function value at θ' using known exact values (e.g., 30°, 45°, 60°).
3. Attach the sign (+ or -) based on the quadrant of θ.
Example: sin 210° → reference 30°, sin 30° = 1/2, Quadrant III sin negative → sin 210° = -1/2.
For coterminal angles outside 0‑360° (or 2π), first reduce by adding/subtracting multiples of 360° (2π).

visuals.title: Evaluating Using Reference Angles

rows.1: Use known exact values of special angles.
Attach sign based on quadrant of original θ.

visuals.caption: The absolute value comes from the reference angle; the sign from the quadrant.

examples.title: Example A — cos(4π/3)
steps: 4π/3 is in Quadrant III → reference angle = 4π/3 - π = π/3.
In Quadrant III, cosine is negative → cos(4π/3) = -1/2.

examples.title: Example B — tan(-210°)
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How do you handle a negative angle? What is the reference angle?
steps: In Quadrant II, tan is negative → tan(-210°) = -√3/3.

examples.title: Example C — csc(11π/4)
steps: In Quadrant II, csc is positive → csc(11π/4) = √2.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Skip the Sign Step
confusionCorner.body: The most common mistake is forgetting to attach the correct sign. Always identify the quadrant of the original angle (after reducing if necessary) before determining the sign.

hints: 330° in Quadrant IV, reference 30°, sin negative.
315° in Quadrant IV, cosine positive, reference 45°.

questions.prompt: Evaluate tan 5π/3. (Use 'sqrt(3)' format with sign if negative.)
hints: 5π/3 in Quadrant IV, reference π/3, tan negative.

blocks.title: Using Identities with Any Angle — Understand → Solve → Conclude
teacherCues: Write the Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Ask: Does this hold for all angles, not just acute? (Yes!)
Given sin θ = 1/3 and θ in Quadrant II, ask: How do we find cos θ? (Use identity, then choose negative root.)

discoveryHook.scenario: A satellite's signal angle gives sin θ = 0.3 with θ in Quadrant II. To decode the signal strength, the onboard computer needs cos θ instantly. Using the identity cos²θ = 1 - sin²θ and knowing the quadrant sign, it computes cos θ = -√(0.91) without any reference angle.

explanation: All trigonometric identities hold for any angle, not just acute angles.
Use the Pythagorean identities: $ \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1 $, $ 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta $, $ 1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta $.
Given one function value and the quadrant, you can find others: solve the identity, then choose the correct sign based on quadrant.
Also use quotient and reciprocal identities as needed.
This method avoids drawing the triangle and works for any angle, even quadrantal.

visuals.title: Using Identities Strategy

rows.1: Identify given function, quadrant, and which function to find.
Use appropriate identity to solve for the unknown function.
Apply quadrant sign to choose correct root; state final value.

visuals.caption: Identities work for all angles; just watch the sign.

formulaCard.title: Pythagorean Identities for Any Angle
notes: Use quadrant to choose sign of root.

examples.title: Example A — Finding cos θ and tan θ
examples.prompt: Given sin θ = 1/3 and θ in Quadrant II, find cos θ and tan θ.
steps: Understand: Need cos θ and tan θ; θ in QII, so cos θ < 0, tan θ < 0.
Solve: Use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 → (1/3)² + cos²θ = 1 → cos²θ = 8/9 → cos θ = -√(8/9) = -2√2/3.
tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = (1/3) / (-2√2/3) = -1/(2√2) = -√2/4 (rationalized).

examples.title: Example B — Using tan to find sec
examples.prompt: Given tan θ = -5/12 and cos θ > 0, find sec θ.
examples.peerPrompt: Which quadrant is θ in? Which identity connects tan and sec?
steps: Understand: tan negative, cos positive → QIV. Need sec θ (positive).

examples.title: Example C — Finding csc θ from cot θ
examples.prompt: Given cot θ = -2 and sin θ < 0, find csc θ.
steps: Understand: cot negative, sin negative → QIV. Need csc θ (negative).

confusionCorner.title: Square Root Sign Choice
confusionCorner.body: When solving an identity, you get two square roots (±). Always use the quadrant information to pick the correct sign. For example, in QII, sine positive, cosine negative.

questions.prompt: If cos θ = -0.6 and θ in Quadrant III, what is sin θ? (Decimal, e.g., 0.8 or -0.8.)
If tan θ = 1 and θ in QIII, sec θ = ___ (use 'sqrt(2)' with sign if needed).
hints: In QIII, x and y negative, so tan positive, sec negative.

questions.prompt: Given sin θ = -3/5 and tan θ > 0, find cos θ. (Fraction like '4/5' or '-4/5'.)
hints: sin negative, tan positive → QIII (both sin and cos negative).
